content:
Bishop's Hill fully demolished, residents did not protest

Su said he received the demolition news at the end of July and immediately contacted Sham Shui Po District Councillors, hoping to preserve the fitness equipment on Wozai Mountain, but quoted their reply that "none of the equipment would be retained". Su said that in previous demolitions he had been able to organise residents to petition and protest, but this time the notice period was too short to organise residents to stop the works, resulting in the morning exercise spot that residents had used for over 20 years finally coming to an end.

Three days ago (the 10th), the Home Affairs Department announced the Wozai Hill Enhancement Plan, under which the government will clear illegal and unsafe structures, facilities or杂物 on the hill in phases, stating that these objects have illegally occupied government land for many years.

Yesterday (the 12th), at around 6:30 in the morning, staff from the Lands Department and uniformed police arrived, cordoning off the area from the foot to the summit of the Tong Yam Street hillside rest garden. Movers then arrived to remove fitness equipment, bicycles, ping-pong tables and other items. Police deployed冲锋车 and pig cage trucks for警戒. Su said this is just a place where residents exercise, and he cannot understand the purpose of the police arrangements: "Officers just stood there, monitoring the whole time. What are we doing now? Are we rioters? Have we broken the law?"

"Morning Exercise Haven" becomes LCSD facilities

Su pointed out that residents raised a total of HK$400,000 to build Bishop's Hill "Morning Exercise Haven", which includes a ping-pong table, fitness equipment, and unofficial hiking trails built decades ago. On the day of demolition, many residents were still doing morning exercises and using the fitness equipment. Several residents expressed deep sorrow at the disappearance of the morning exercise spot they had used for years. Some residents kept asking Mr Su what to do, but Mr Su also did not know what to do.

He said he had spent several consecutive days moving the fitness equipment away, hoping to preserve the fruits of his labour as much as possible. He has now removed all the muscle massage rollers, while some residents plan to relocate some of the statues to Lantau Island.

According to the Home Affairs Department's Wozai Hill Enhancement Plan, the "Morning Exercise Haven" will be turned into LCSD facilities; the home-made fitness equipment on the hill will be replaced with standard LCSD recreational and sports equipment; as for the statues, religious leaders will visit the site to handle them properly.

Surviving a near-death experience, building Bishop's Hill "Morning Exercise Haven"

75-year-old Su Chi-keung is a SARS survivor. Due to medication side effects, he suffered后遗症 including muscle pain, weakness and fatigue. After three years of physiotherapy, his condition had not improved. In 2008, Su was invited by a neighbour to Bishop's Hill, and after morning exercise he found his spirits improved, which he attributed to the fresh air on the hill. He then began exercising on Bishop's Hill at six every morning. After persisting for a month, he regained his health and strength, and decided to stop physiotherapy.

In 2009, Mr Su travelled to South Korea and was inspired by the local fitness facilities. After returning to Hong Kong, he referenced the designs and hand-made exercise bikes and rope-pulling machines in his own hardware factory, then carried the disassembled fitness equipment up Bishop's Hill by himself. He described the manufacturing as simple, but the process of hauling them up the hill as extremely difficult. As a result, he spent four years building over 20 recreational and sports facilities on Bishop's Hill, including swings, balance bars and rollers, and placed them on the open space above the current Sham Shui Po service reservoir. At the time some elderly residents opposed him, but after residents used the fitness facilities and found relief from physical ailments, the facilities became very popular.

Bishop's Hill first exposed to public eye, residents protest against demolition

Su said that in 2014, over 200 young people held a psychedelic party on Bishop's Hill, creating a noise nuisance. When police arrived, they discovered for the first time a large number of private fitness facilities. Subsequently, the Water Supplies Department increased patrols of Bishop's Hill and repeatedly drove away residents exercising there, and planned to demolish the facilities. At that time, Mr Su organised several protests and went in person to the Sham Shui Po District Council Secretariat to fight for the retention of the fitness garden.

Accidental check-in: Bishop's Hill reservoir becomes a Grade I historic building

In 2017, the Water Supplies Department planned to clear the unauthorised structures on Bishop's Hill and return the land to the Lands Department. In addition, the roots of two large trees on top of the reservoir were extending into the interior, posing a collapse risk. In 2020, preparations were made to remove the trees and fill in the reservoir. The Water Supplies Department promised Mr Su that his fitness facilities could be placed on the filled-in open space, so Su agreed to the works.

As a result, on Christmas Eve, Mr Su and a volunteer sneaked into the reservoir to check if anything was left behind, took photos and posted them on social media. This attracted large crowds to check in at the reservoir, drawing public attention. Su said that at the time, the public protested against demolishing the reservoir because of its historical value. One resident who often visited Bishop's Hill, Fong Jie, even stood in front of an excavator to stop the demolition works.

In 2021, the reservoir was assessed as a Grade I historic building by the Antiquities Advisory Committee. The reservoir was preserved and opened to the public. Mr Su moved his fitness facilities to the foot of the hill.

The Mao Zedong statue incident may have triggered the demolition

In June 2022, the Sham Shui Po District Management Committee wanted to remove the altar and fitness facilities. Mr Su launched a petition to fight for retention, saying a total of 3,399 Sham Shui Po district residents signed it, and he delivered the letter to the Home Affairs Department, promising not to expand the facilities further.

Su said that after that, Bishop's Hill remained stable, and the government did not say it had to be cleared. However, in early 2026, resident Fong Jie set up a Mao Zedong statue and a Mao Zedong cultural hall on Bishop's Hill. Although they were later removed, Su believes the Mao Zedong incident rekindled the government's attention to Bishop's Hill. Coupled with some residents making a lot of noise on the hill and disturbing nearby residents, the government decided to completely clear Bishop's Hill.

In early 2026, resident Fong Jie set up a Mao Zedong statue and a Mao Zedong cultural hall on Bishop's Hill, reigniting controversy over the use of the hill. (File photo)

"Without Bishop's Hill, I would have lived 20 years less"

Watching workers dismantle the fitness equipment he had built piece by piece, Su did not show sadness. He plans to take the dismantled fitness equipment back to his ancestral home, and he has been telling the media about the history of Bishop's Hill. In fact, he is well aware that the "Morning Exercise Haven" has been in violation for years and is highly controversial, but he believes this place has benefited many residents. He hopes that by telling the story of Bishop's Hill, he can gain the government's recognition. Although ultimately it was not preserved, he still wants to pass the story on, to repay Bishop's Hill for the grace it has shown him.

He bade farewell to Bishop's Hill: "I am grateful it gave me a new life. Without it I wouldn't have those 20 years, I should have died. If it weren't for Bishop's Hill, I would be dead... Besides, I am a SARS survivor who was injured, do you think I could have lived to today?"
